einzeiler: Investigating decades of unsolved murders of women across Chicago.
kurzfassung: Over the course of two decades, dozens of women were found strangled, beaten, or abandoned in alleys and vacant buildings throughout Chicago. While families and journalists worked to connect the cases and demand answers, many of the investigations remained stalled without identified suspects. The episode honors the victims' lives and highlights the systemic neglect faced by vulnerable women in the city.
stichpunkte: Dozens of women were discovered murdered in Chicago alleys, abandoned buildings, and garbage cans starting in the late 1990s.
Many victims shared vulnerabilities such as struggling with drug addiction or being involved in sex work.
Families of the victims were often the first to notice chilling similarities between the separate murder cases.
Investigative journalism by the Chicago Tribune in 2018 brought widespread attention to the high number of unsolved strangulation cases.
Organizations like the Murder Accountability Project pointed to low clearance rates and potential serial offender patterns.
Despite DNA testing and police case reviews, the vast majority of these homicides remain officially unsolved.

clips.hook: Dozens of women dying in the same city
clips.text: The speakers express shock at the sheer volume of women losing their lives in rapid succession within a single urban area.

clips.hook: The flawed assumption that victims left by choice
clips.text: Frustration is raised regarding authorities frequently dismissing missing women by claiming they chose to walk away from their stable lives.

clips.hook: The agonizing reality of how long strangulation takes
clips.text: A comparison to a trial tracking the exact duration of oxygen deprivation emphasizes the immense cruelty and deliberate nature of the crime.
The hosts express astonishment upon learning that numerous separate DNA profiles were recovered from the crime scenes without yielding matches.

clips.hook: Why the victims' humanity matters most
clips.text: The hosts emphasize the importance of speaking the names and restoring humanity to the victims whose lives were treated as disposable.

beschreibung:
Between 2001 and 2017, at least 75 women were strangled or smothered in Chicago. Many were found in alleys, vacant buildings, garbage cans, and other places where it was easy for their deaths to become separate case files instead of a citywide emergency. The women were daughters, mothers, artists, business owners, caregivers, and friends. Their names included Angela Ford, Gwendolyn Williams, Nancy Walker, Margaret Gomez, Teresa Bunn, Hazel Lewis, and Rio Renee Holyfield.

In 2018, the Chicago Tribune identified 75 women whose cases showed a devastating pattern. 25 cases had been closed, while more than two thirds remained unsolved. Families and advocates had long questioned whether some of the murders were connected. The term "Chicago Strangler" became shorthand for those fears, but Chicago police have said there is no evidence that one person killed every woman in the group. The available evidence points to an even more difficult possibility: some cases may be linked, some may involve multiple offenders, and far too many families are still waiting for answers.

We discuss the women at the heart of these cases, the investigation that revealed the scale of the failures, and the work advocates continue to do to make sure they are not forgotten.
